claim: Maf and Mafb transcription factors have compensatory roles in repressing somatostatin (SST+) interneuron production in medial ganglionic eminence (MGE) secondary progenitors in mice.
source: Maf (c-Maf) and Mafb transcription factors (TFs) have compensatory roles in repressing somatostatin (SST+) interneuron (IN) production in medial ganglionic eminence (MGE) secondary progenitors in mice.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by previous work (Pai et al., 2019) referenced throughout the manuscript.

claim: Maf and Mafb conditional deletion (cDKO) decreases the survival of MGE-derived cortical interneurons (CINs).
source: Maf and Mafb conditional deletion (cDKO) decreases the survival of MGE-derived cortical interneurons (CINs) and changes their physiological properties.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data from previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Maf and Mafb conditional deletion changes the physiological properties of MGE-derived cortical interneurons.
source: Maf and Mafb conditional deletion (cDKO) decreases the survival of MGE-derived cortical interneurons (CINs) and changes their physiological properties.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data from previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Mef2c and Snap25 are positively regulated by Maf and Mafb to drive interneuron morphological maturation.
source: Herein, we show that (1) Mef2c and Snap25 are positively regulated by Maf and Mafb to drive IN morphological maturation
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing rescue of neurite outgrowth defects.

claim: Maf and Mafb promote Mef2c expression which specifies parvalbumin (PV+) interneurons.
source: (2) Maf and Mafb promote Mef2c expression which specifies parvalbumin (PV+) INs
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 2 showing rescue of PV+ IN production by Mef2c transfection.

claim: Elmo1, Igfbp4 and Mef2c are candidate markers of immature PV+ hippocampal interneurons.
source: (3) Elmo1, Igfbp4 and Mef2c are candidate markers of immature PV+ hippocampal INs (HIN).
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by RNAscope data in Figure 3 showing differential expression in Sst- vs Sst+ populations.

claim: Maf/Mafb neonatal cDKOs have decreased cortical interneurons.
source: Furthermore, Maf/Mafb neonatal cDKOs have decreased CINs and increased HINs, that express Pnoc, an HIN specific marker.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by quantification data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Maf/Mafb neonatal cDKOs have increased hippocampal interneurons that express Pnoc.
source: Furthermore, Maf/Mafb neonatal cDKOs have decreased CINs and increased HINs, that express Pnoc, an HIN specific marker.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by quantification data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Pnoc is a hippocampal interneuron specific marker.
source: Furthermore, Maf/Mafb neonatal cDKOs have decreased CINs and increased HINs, that express Pnoc, an HIN specific marker.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by FISH data in Figure 5 showing Pnoc expression is largely restricted to hippocampus.

claim: Interneuron pathologies are hypothesized to underlie symptoms of autism spectrum disorder, epilepsy and schizophrenia.
source: IN pathologies are hypothesized to underlie symptoms of neurological and neuropsychiatric disorders such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), epilepsy and schizophrenia.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature (Lim et al., 2018; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011).

claim: Interneuron pathology leads to disrupted circuit inhibition, resulting in circuit hyperexcitability and less efficient information processing.
source: One possible explanation is that IN pathology leads to disrupted circuit inhibition, resulting in circuit hyperexcitability and less efficient information processing (Lim et al., 2018; Rubenstein and Merzenich, 2003; Sohal and Rubenstein, 2019; Yizhar et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cortical interneurons are generated in three subpallial progenitor domains: the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences (MGE and CGE), and the preotic area (POA).
source: CINs are generated in three subpallial progenitor domains: the medial and caudal ganglionic eminences (MGE and CGE), and the preotic area (POA) (Gelman et al., 2011; Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature (Gelman et al., 2011; Lim et al., 2018).

claim: MGE and POA-derived cortical interneurons express parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (SST).
source: MGE and POA-derived CINs express parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (SST), while CGE-derived CINs express either vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), cholecystokinin (CCK) or reelin [but lack SST].
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: CGE-derived cortical interneurons express either vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), cholecystokinin (CCK) or reelin but lack SST.
source: MGE and POA-derived CINs express parvalbumin (PV) or somatostatin (SST), while CGE-derived CINs express either vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP), cholecystokinin (CCK) or reelin [but lack SST].
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: Hippocampal interneurons are generated by the same general progenitor pools as cortical interneurons and share similar molecular properties.
source: HINs are generated by the same general progenitor pools and share similar molecular properties with CINs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: There are no clear single markers known to define developing or mature hippocampal interneurons from cortical interneurons.
source: However, so far there are no clear single markers that are known to define developing or mature HINs from CINs (Pelkey et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous literature (Pelkey et al., 2017).

claim: Maf and Mafb function together in the MGE to control the timing and quantity of SST+ cortical interneurons that are generated.
source: We have recently demonstrated that two Maf TFs, Maf (c-Maf) and Mafb, function together in the MGE to control the timing and quantity of SST+ CINs that are generated (Pai et al., 2019), schematically summarized in Schemes 1–3.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of Mafb and Maf in the Nkx2.1-Cre lineage leads to the overproduction of SST+ cortical interneurons at the expense of PV+ cortical interneurons.
source: Loss of Mafb and Maf in the Nkx2.1-Cre lineage (Maf cDKO) leads to the overproduction of SST+ CINs at the expense of PV+ CINs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Maf cDKOs have reduced cortical interneurons (~30%) at P0.
source: Maf cDKOs also have changes in the quantity and distribution of the total Nkx2.1-cre lineage INs: reduced CINs (~30%) and increased HINs (~2 fold) at P0, and a progressive loss of INs that plateaued by adulthood at ~70% reduction (Schemes 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Maf cDKOs have increased hippocampal interneurons (~2 fold) at P0.
source: Maf cDKOs also have changes in the quantity and distribution of the total Nkx2.1-cre lineage INs: reduced CINs (~30%) and increased HINs (~2 fold) at P0, and a progressive loss of INs that plateaued by adulthood at ~70% reduction (Schemes 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Maf cDKOs have a progressive loss of interneurons that plateaued by adulthood at ~70% reduction.
source: Maf cDKOs also have changes in the quantity and distribution of the total Nkx2.1-cre lineage INs: reduced CINs (~30%) and increased HINs (~2 fold) at P0, and a progressive loss of INs that plateaued by adulthood at ~70% reduction (Schemes 1 and 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Loss of Maf and Mafb alters postnatal cortical interneuron properties, including process morphogenesis, synaptogenesis, intrinsic electrophysiology and circuit excitability.
source: Loss of Maf and Mafb also alters postnatal CIN properties, including process morphogenesis, synaptogenesis, intrinsic electrophysiology and circuit excitability (Pai et al., 2019; Schemes 2 and 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Adult Maf cDKOs have spontaneous non-motor epileptic activity.
source: Furthermore, adult Maf cDKOs have spontaneous non-motor epileptic activity, likely associated with the interneuronopathy (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by EEG recording data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single cell RNA-sequencing identified 24 different clusters from P0 WT and cDKO neocortices, including excitatory neurons, neural progenitors, microglia as well as MGE and CGE-derived interneurons.
source: We identified 24 different clusters, including excitatory neurons, neural progenitors, microglia as well as MGE and CGE-derived INs, which were visualized by uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) (Figure 1B and C; Becht et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by UMAP visualization in Figure 1B and C.

claim: MGE-derived interneurons were in cluster 1, based on marker gene co-expression, including LIM homeobox 6 (Lhx6), Maf, Mafb and neurexophilin 1 (Nxph1).
source: MGE-derived INs were in cluster 1, based on marker gene co-expression, including LIM homeobox 6 (Lhx6), Maf, Mafb and neurexophilin 1 (Nxph1) (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by expression data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: Nxph1 is specifically expressed within the Nkx2.1-lineage.
source: We performed fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) to confirm the specificity of Nxph1 expression within the Nkx2.1-lineage by co-labeling Nxph1 and Nkx2.1-Cre driven tdTomato (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: There were no obvious transcriptomic changes in neural progenitors, excitatory neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia and the CGE-derived interneuron population between WT and cDKO.
source: There were no obvious transcriptomic changes in neural progenitors, excitatory neurons, oligodendrocytes, microglia and the CGE-derived IN population between WT and cDKO (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by UMAP visualization in Figure 1B and C showing no separation of WT and cDKO cells in non-MGE clusters.

claim: Loss of Maf and Mafb in the Nkx2.1-Cre-lineage has no gross non-cell autonomous effects.
source: This suggests no gross non-cell autonomous effects exerted by loss of Maf and Mafb in the Nkx2.1-Cre-lineage.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the lack of transcriptomic changes in non-MGE cell populations.

claim: The MGE-derived interneuron population (cluster 1) showed clear differences between WT and cDKO.
source: However, the MGE-derived IN population (cluster 1) showed clear differences between WT and cDKO (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by UMAP visualization in Figure 1C showing separation of WT and cDKO cells in cluster 1.

claim: Differential gene expression analysis in MGE-derived interneurons identified 81 differentially expressed genes, with 47 upregulated and 34 down-regulated in the Maf cDKO.
source: We performed differential gene expression (DEX) analysis in this MGE-derived IN cluster, and identified 81 differentially expressed (DE) genes, with 47 upregulated (including Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc and Neuropeptide Y) and 34 down-regulated (including Maf, Mafb, Neurexophilin2, Mef2c, Cxcr4 and Snap25) in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Upregulated genes in Maf cDKO MGE-derived interneurons include Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc and Neuropeptide Y.
source: We performed differential gene expression (DEX) analysis in this MGE-derived IN cluster, and identified 81 differentially expressed (DE) genes, with 47 upregulated (including Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc and Neuropeptide Y) and 34 down-regulated (including Maf, Mafb, Neurexophilin2, Mef2c, Cxcr4 and Snap25) in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Down-regulated genes in Maf cDKO MGE-derived interneurons include Maf, Mafb, Neurexophilin2, Mef2c, Cxcr4 and Snap25.
source: We performed differential gene expression (DEX) analysis in this MGE-derived IN cluster, and identified 81 differentially expressed (DE) genes, with 47 upregulated (including Sst, Nrp1, Pnoc and Neuropeptide Y) and 34 down-regulated (including Maf, Mafb, Neurexophilin2, Mef2c, Cxcr4 and Snap25) in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Gene ontology analysis showed that most dysregulated genes are involved in synapse formation, neurite projection and neuronal maturation.
source: Gene ontology analysis, based upon cellular components, showed that most dysregulated genes are involved in synapse formation, neurite projection and neuronal maturation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by gene ontology analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Mef2c was the third most down-regulated gene in Maf cDKO MGE derived interneurons.
source: Based on DEX analysis, Mef2c was the third most down-regulated gene, while Sst was the most upregulated gene (Figure 1F–G, S7).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis.

claim: Sst was the most upregulated gene in Maf cDKO MGE derived interneurons.
source: Based on DEX analysis, Mef2c was the third most down-regulated gene, while Sst was the most upregulated gene (Figure 1F–G, S7).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis.

claim: MEF2C expression was reduced in tdTomato+ cortical interneurons across all cortical layers in P2 cDKOs.
source: To validate the Mef2c result, we used immunofluorescence labeling; MEF2C expression was reduced in the tdTomato+ CINs across all cortical layers in the P2 cDKOs (Figure 1F and L–N) (Bin 3, 4, 7: p<0.05; Bin 5, 6: p<0.01; Density: p<0.01; Welch's t test)
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1L-N with statistical analysis.

claim: P2 cDKOs have increased Sst ISH signal and increased numbers of Sst+ cortical interneurons.
source: To validate the Sst result, we used FISH; we found both increased Sst ISH signal and increased numbers of Sst+ CINs at P2 in cDKOs as before (Figure 1G and H–J) (Sst density: p=0.0001, Welch's t test) (Pai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1H-J with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a > 3 fold increase in Sst and EdU double labeled cortical interneurons in P2 cDKO neocortices born at E15.5.
source: There was a > 3 fold increase in Sst and EdU double labeled CINs in P2 cDKO neocortices (Figure 1K) (Sst-EdU density: p<0.0001; Welch's t test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 1K with statistical analysis.

claim: Maf cDKOs overproduce Sst+ cortical interneurons across development.
source: Thus, Maf cDKOs overproduce Sst+ CINs across development.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the EdU labeling experiments showing increased Sst+ CINs at multiple developmental time points.

claim: Prenatal loss of Mef2c reduces the number of PV+ cortical interneurons.
source: Prenatal loss of Mef2c reduces the number of PV+ CINs (Mayer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citation to previous literature (Mayer et al., 2018).

claim: Maf and Mafb are genetically upstream of Mef2c.
source: Given our finding that Mef2c expression is reduced in Maf cDKOs (Figure 1), it suggests that Maf and Mafb are genetically upstream of Mef2c.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the observation that Mef2c expression is reduced in Maf cDKOs.

claim: Deficits in Mef2c potentially underlie the mechanisms causal to the PV+ cortical interneuron loss in the Maf cDKO.
source: We thus hypothesized that deficits in Mef2c potentially underlie the mechanisms causal to the PV+ CIN loss in the Maf cDKO (this report; Pai et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section based on the observation that Mef2c is reduced in cDKOs and that Mef2c loss reduces PV+ INs.

claim: Maf cDKO MGE cells have reduced PV+ cortical interneurons in transplantation assays.
source: The analysis confirmed the preferential loss of PV+ CINs in the cDKOs (Pai et al., 2019; Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Mef2c transfection rescued the PV+ cortical interneuron deficit in Maf cDKO MGE cells.
source: Importantly, we found that Mef2c transfection rescued this phenotype, and corrected the SST/PV ratio (Figure 2B and K) (PV population: WT vs. cDKO p<0.0001; cDKO vs. cDKO+Mef2c p<0.0001; Chi-square test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 2B and K with statistical analysis.

claim: Maf and Mafb promote Mef2c expression, which in turn promotes the PV+ interneuron fate.
source: Together, these data suggest that Maf and Mafb promote Mef2c expression, which in turn promotes the PV+ IN fate (Figure 2—figure supplement 1. Model).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the rescue experiments showing that Mef2c can restore PV+ IN production in cDKOs.

claim: Within MGE-derived interneurons, the Sst-negative (Sst-) group primarily comprises the future PV+ interneurons.
source: We hypothesize that within MGE-derived INs, the Sst-negative (Sst-) group primarily comprises the future PV+ INs, in part since Sst-IRES-Cre lineage tracing showed that the majority of the SST+ INs remain SST+ (Pai et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a hypothesis stated in the results section based on Sst-IRES-Cre lineage tracing data.

claim: Sst-IRES-Cre lineage tracing showed that the majority of the SST+ interneurons remain SST+.
source: We hypothesize that within MGE-derived INs, the Sst-negative (Sst-) group primarily comprises the future PV+ INs, in part since Sst-IRES-Cre lineage tracing showed that the majority of the SST+ INs remain SST+ (Pai et al., 2019; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Arl4d, Elmo1, Igfbp4, Mef2c, Sp9 and Tcf12 are enriched in the Sst- MGE-derived interneuron population.
source: We identified a group of genes that are enriched in the Sst- population, by comparing the IN marker expression between the two groups (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2). From these, we selected six genes, ADP ribosylation factor like GTPase 4D (Arl4d), engulfment and cell motility protein 1 (Elmo1), insulin like growth factor binding protein 4 (Igfbp4), Mef2c, Sp9 and transcription factor 12 (Tcf12), with high-to-moderate expression to evaluate their RNA expression.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by scRNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mef2c is a very specific Sst- population marker, especially in the hippocampus.
source: Our results suggested that Mef2c is a very specific Sst- population marker, especially in the hippocampus (Cortex: p<0.05; Hippocampus: p<0.0001).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: Elmo1, Igfbp4, and Sp9 are good markers for Sst- MGE-derived interneurons in the hippocampus.
source: Likewise, Elmo1, Igfbp4, and Sp9 appear to be good markers for Sst- MGE-derived INs in the hippocampus (Elmo1: p<0.001; Igfbp4: p<0.05; Tcf12: p<0.01; unpaired test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by RNAscope data shown in Figure 3 with statistical analysis.

claim: This is the first study to identify genes that are almost exclusively expressed in Sst- MGE-derived immature hippocampal interneurons.
source: This likely is the first study to identify genes, such as Mef2c, that are almost exclusively expressed in Sst- MGE-derived immature HINs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and represents a novel finding of the study.

claim: Reduced expression of Mef2c and Snap25 impedes neurite morphogenesis.
source: Reduced expression of Mef2c and Snap25 was shown to impede neurite morphogenesis (Harrington et al., 2016; Houenou et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous literature (Harrington et al., 2016; Houenou et al., 2017; Tu et al., 2017).

claim: Maf cDKOs have a neurite outgrowth defect in vitro and in vivo.
source: Since Maf cDKOs have a neurite outgrowth defect in vitro and in vivo (Pai et al., 2019, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we examined whether the decreased expression of Mef2c and Snap25 in the cDKOs underlies their neurite outgrowth defect (Pai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citation to previous work (Pai et al., 2019) and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: cDKO cortical interneurons had decreased numbers of neurites.
source: As before, cDKO CINs had decreased numbers of neurites; Gfp transfection did not alter this phenotype (Figure 4B, C and G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Transfection of cDKO with Maf, Mef2c or Snap25 rescued neurite numbers to levels comparable to WT.
source: Second, transfection of cDKO with Maf, Mef2c or Snap25 rescued neurite numbers, and the increased neurite numbers were comparable to WT (Figure 4B, D–F and H–I).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Reduced Mef2c and Snap25 expression are downstream of Maf and Mafb in regulating neurite complexity in neonatal cortical interneurons.
source: These results provide evidence that reduced Mef2c and Snap25 expression are downstream of Maf and Mafb in regulating neurite complexity in neonatal CINs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claim: Sst-IRES-Cre generated Maf cDKO interneurons have neurite defects similar to those found using Nkx2.1-Cre.
source: We found that the Sst-IRES-Cre generated Maf cDKO had neurite defects similar to those found using Nkx2.1-Cre.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Maf function in neurite outgrowth is required post-mitotically.
source: Thus, Maf function in neurite outgrowth is also required post-mitotically.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the Sst-IRES-Cre experiments showing neurite defects when Maf is deleted post-mitotically.

claim: Postnatal deletion of Maf and Mafb in cortical interneurons (cDKOPOST) resulted in reduced neurite complexity.
source: At DIV14, we performed Sholl analysis, which revealed that cDKOPOST INs had reduced neurite complexity, providing evidence that Maf and Mafb regulate IN morphology postnatally.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Maf and Mafb regulate interneuron morphology postnatally.
source: At DIV14, we performed Sholl analysis, which revealed that cDKOPOST INs had reduced neurite complexity, providing evidence that Maf and Mafb regulate IN morphology postnatally.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the postnatal deletion experiments.

claim: Maf, Mef2c and Snap25 each rescued the neurite outgrowth defect in postnatal Maf cDKO interneurons.
source: Maf, Mef2c and Snap25 each rescued the neurite outgrowth defect (Figure 4K–R).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by Sholl analysis data shown in Figure 4K-R.

claim: Maf and Mafb likely promote cortical interneuron neurite morphogenesis at postnatal stages through Mef2c and Snap25.
source: Thus, Maf and Mafb likely promote CIN neurite morphogenesis at postnatal stages through Mef2c and Snap25.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the postnatal rescue experiments.

claim: Prepronociceptin (Pnoc) was an upregulated gene in the Maf cDKO.
source: The DEX analysis revealed that prepronociceptin (Pnoc) was an upregulated gene in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Pnoc is a marker of O-LM interneurons, a subtype that is mainly Sst+.
source: A recent study focusing on adult CA1 HIN profiling suggested Pnoc is a marker of O-LM INs, a subtype that is mainly Sst+ (Harris et al., 2018; Asgarian et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous literature (Harris et al., 2018; Asgarian et al., 2019).

claim: In P2 WTs, Pnoc+ cells were largely restricted to the hippocampus.
source: In P2 WTs, Pnoc+ cells were largely restricted to the hippocampus (Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: ~40% of the Pnoc+ hippocampal interneurons are tdTomato+ (Nkx2.1-Cre lineage).
source: ~40% of the Pnoc+ HINs are tdTomato+; very few of them are Htr3a+ (CGE marker), suggesting that the MGE/POA is the main origin of these HINs ((Figure 5I–M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Very few Pnoc+ hippocampal interneurons are Htr3a+ (CGE marker).
source: ~40% of the Pnoc+ HINs are tdTomato+; very few of them are Htr3a+ (CGE marker), suggesting that the MGE/POA is the main origin of these HINs ((Figure 5I–M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The MGE/POA is the main origin of Pnoc+ hippocampal interneurons.
source: ~40% of the Pnoc+ HINs are tdTomato+; very few of them are Htr3a+ (CGE marker), suggesting that the MGE/POA is the main origin of these HINs ((Figure 5I–M, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the observation that many Pnoc+ HINs are tdTomato+ (MGE/POA lineage) and few are Htr3a+ (CGE lineage).

claim: In the Maf cDKO there was ectopic Pnoc expression in the neocortex, highest in the dorsomedial regions abutting the hippocampus.
source: In the Maf cDKO there was ectopic Pnoc expression in the neocortex (highest in the dorsomedial regions abutting the hippocampus), as well as increased Pnoc+ cells in the hippocampus, consistent with an increased density of HINs (Figure 5A–L) (WT vs cDKO: Neocortex p<0.01; dorsomedial Neocortex p<0.0001; Hippocampus p<0.01; t test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5A-L with statistical analysis.

claim: Maf cDKO has increased Pnoc+ cells in the hippocampus.
source: In the Maf cDKO there was ectopic Pnoc expression in the neocortex (highest in the dorsomedial regions abutting the hippocampus), as well as increased Pnoc+ cells in the hippocampus, consistent with an increased density of HINs (Figure 5A–L) (WT vs cDKO: Neocortex p<0.01; dorsomedial Neocortex p<0.0001; Hippocampus p<0.01; t test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5A-L with statistical analysis.

claim: Sst FISH and tdTomato+ interneuron quantifications both suggested increased hippocampal interneuron density in the Maf cDKO.
source: Indeed, Sst FISH and tdTomato+ IN quantifications both suggested increased HIN density in the Maf cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 7, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH and quantification data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Loss of Maf and Mafb leads to increased production of hippocampal interneurons, which are mainly Sst+ and/or Pnoc+.
source: Together, these data provide evidence that loss of Maf and Mafb leads to increased production of HINs, which are mainly Sst+ and/or Pnoc+.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the FISH data showing increased Sst+ and Pnoc+ HINs in cDKOs.

claim: Lhx6+ cortical interneuron density was decreased in Maf cDKOs at P2.
source: Lhx6+ CIN density was decreased in Maf cDKOs as previously reported (Pai et al., 2019; Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: There was an increased density of Lhx6+ hippocampal interneurons across all hippocampal regions in the Maf cDKO at P2.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, there was an increased density of Lhx6+ HINs across all hippocampal regions in the Maf cDKO (p<0.05; Welch's t test) (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 6C with statistical analysis.

claim: There was an increased density of Sst+ hippocampal interneurons in all hippocampal regions in the Maf cDKO at P2.
source: Furthermore, there was an increased density of Sst+ HINs cell density in all hippocampal regions (CA1:~1.5 fold; p<0.001, CA3 and DG:~2 fold; p<0.0001) (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FISH quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7 with statistical analysis.

claim: At E12.5, Maf cDKOs showed ~2 fold increase in hippocampal interneuron generation.
source: At E12.5 (early-born; Lhx6+;BrdU+), we observed ~2 fold increase in HIN generation in the Maf cDKO (p<0.01; t test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in hippocampal interneuron generation at E12.5 was similar across all hippocampal subregions in Maf cDKOs.
source: The increase was similar across all hippocampal subregions (Figure 6D, E, H and I) (CA1: p=0.02; CA3: p<0.001; DG: p<0.01; t test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: Maf cDKOs had a trend toward decreased cortical interneuron generation at E12.5.
source: In contrast, Maf cDKOs had a trend toward decreased CIN generation at E12.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by BrdU labeling data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: At E15.5, Maf cDKOs showed ~2.5 fold increase in hippocampal interneuron production.
source: At E15.5 (late-born; Lhx6+;EdU+), we observed ~2.5 fold increase in HIN production (p<0.0001; t test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in hippocampal interneuron production at E15.5 was across all hippocampal subregions in Maf cDKOs.
source: Similarly, the increase was across all hippocampal subregions (Figure 6F, G, J and K) (CA1: p<0.001; CA3: p<0.05; DG: p<0.01; t test).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: In WTs, the MGE tends to generate hippocampal interneurons/cortical interneurons in a 1:2 ratio at both E12.5 and E15.5.
source: In WTs, the MGE tends to generate HINs/CINs in a 1:2 ratio at both E12.5 and E15.5.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In cDKOs, the MGE overproduces hippocampal interneurons, especially at E12.5.
source: In cDKOs, the MGE overproduces HINs, especially at E12.5 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Maf and Mafb leads to hippocampal interneuron overproduction perhaps at the expense of generating cortical interneurons.
source: Together, these data support the hypothesis that loss of Maf and Mafb leads to HIN overproduction perhaps at the expense of generating CINs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is inferred from the birth-dating experiments showing increased HIN and decreased CIN generation.

claim: Mef2c is a high confidence risk gene for ASD, intellectual disability and schizophrenia.
source: Mef2c is a high confidence risk gene for ASD, intellectual disability(ID) and schizophrenia (Tu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Tu et al., 2017).

claim: Mef2c has roles in promoting cortical excitatory neuron synapse formation and morphology maturation.
source: Notably, Mef2c has roles in promoting cortical excitatory neuron synapse formation and morphology maturation (Harrington et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Harrington et al., 2016).

claim: Mef2c marks PV interneuron precursors and is required for PV interneuron development.
source: Furthermore, there is evidence that Mef2c marks PV IN precursors, and is required for PV IN development (Mayer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Mayer et al., 2018).

claim: Mef2c promotes interneuron morphological maturation, similar to its functions in excitatory neurons.
source: Mef2c rescued the IN neurite outgrowth defect of both prenatal and postnatal Maf cDKO INs (Figure 4). Thus, Mef2c promotes IN morphological maturation, similar to its functions in excitatory neurons (Harrington et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the rescue experiments and comparison to previous literature.

claim: Deletion of Mef2c using Dlx5/6-Cre led to a preferential loss of PV cortical interneurons, similar to the Maf cDKO phenotype.
source: Deletion of Mef2c using Dlx5/6-Cre led to a preferential loss of PV CINs, similar to the Maf cDKO phenotype (Mayer et al., 2018; Pai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature (Mayer et al., 2018; Pai et al., 2019).

claim: Transduction of Mef2c into Maf cDKO MGE cells largely rescued their deficit in generating PV cortical interneurons.
source: Here we found that transduction of Mef2c into Maf cDKO MGE cells largely rescued their deficit in generating PV CINs (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by transplantation data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The Maf cDKO MGE generates ~2 fold increase in SST+ cortical interneurons born at E12.5 and at E15.5, probably at the expense of generating PV+ cortical interneurons.
source: The Maf cDKO MGE generates ~2 fold increase in SST+ CINs born at E12.5 and at E15.5, probably at the expense of generating PV+ CINs (Figure 1; Pai et al., 2019; Scheme 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by EdU labeling data shown in Figure 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: In the absence of the Maf genes, the MGE has a persistent defect in generating the proper balance of SST/PV interneurons.
source: Thus, in the absence of the Maf genes, the MGE has a persistent defect in generating the proper balance of SST/PV INs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the observation that SST+ CIN overproduction occurs at multiple developmental time points.

claim: A transcriptional pathway exists in which Maf and/or Mafb drive Mef2c expression in MGE progenitors to promote PV interneuron production.
source: We propose a transcriptional pathway in which Maf and/or Mafb drive Mef2c expression in MGE progenitors to promote PV IN production (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a proposed model stated in the discussion based on the experimental findings.

claim: The Maf/Mafb→Mef2c transcriptional pathway may operate in conjunction with signaling hubs such as MTOR/MAPK/RYK.
source: This pathway may operate in conjunction with signaling hubs such as MTOR/MAPK/RYK, as perturbation in these pathways also lead to altered PV/SST expression (Malik et al., 2019; McKenzie et al., 2019; Angara et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative claim stated in the discussion based on comparison to other studies.

claim: Cellular signaling as well as the Mafs and Mef2c are critical components of the program driving PV interneuron development.
source: Thus, cellular signaling as well as the Mafs and Mef2c are critical components of the program driving PV IN development.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the experimental findings and comparison to other studies.

claim: Maf, Mafb and Mef2c expression persist as interneurons migrate into and mature in the pallium.
source: Maf, Mafb and Mef2c expression persist as INs migrate into and mature in the pallium.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is based on the observation that these genes are expressed in postnatal INs.

claim: Neonatal deletion of Maf and Mafb led to reduced neurite outgrowth, a defect rescued by Mef2c transduction.
source: Neonatal deletion of Maf and Mafb led to reduced neurite outgrowth, a defect rescued by Mef2c transduction (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The proposed Maf/Mafb→Mef2c transcription pathway persists as interneurons mature postnatally.
source: Thus, our proposed Maf/Mafb→ Mef2c transcription pathway persists as INs mature postnatally.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the postnatal rescue experiments.

claim: Snap25 is part of the neuronal SNAP receptor (SNARE) complex which regulates vesicle fusion, receptor trafficking and neurite branching.
source: Snap25 is part of the neuronal SNAP receptor (SNARE) complex which regulates vesicle fusion, receptor trafficking and neurite branching (Delgado-Martínez et al., 2007; Sudhof, 2004).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature (Delgado-Martínez et al., 2007; Sudhof, 2004).

claim: Snap25 loss of function in hippocampal excitatory neurons causes defects in neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival.
source: Snap25 loss of function studies in hippocampal excitatory neurons causes defects in neurite outgrowth and neuronal survival (Delgado-Martínez et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Delgado-Martínez et al., 2007).

claim: Snap25 expression was decreased in the Maf cDKO interneurons.
source: Snap25 expression was decreased in the Maf cDKO INs (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Expressing Snap25 in prenatal and postnatal Maf cDKO interneurons rescued their neurite outgrowth defect, similar to what was observed with Mef2c.
source: Expressing Snap25 in prenatal and postnatal Maf cDKO INs, rescued their neurite outgrowth defect, similar to what was observed with Mef2c (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Maf and Mafb driven expression of both Snap25 and Mef2c are critical aspects of how the Maf genes regulate interneuron development.
source: Thus, Maf and Mafb driven expression of both Snap25 and Mef2c are critical aspects of how the Maf genes regulate IN development.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the rescue experiments.

claim: Snap25 and Mef2c may regulate each other since each gene could rescue the neurite outgrowth phenotype.
source: Since each gene could rescue these phenotypes, it is possible that they may regulate each other.
evidence: This is a speculative claim stated in the discussion based on the observation that both genes can rescue the phenotype.

claim: The molecular program that distinguishes cortical interneurons from hippocampal interneurons generated by the MGE remains largely unknown.
source: The molecular program that distinguishes CINs from HINs generated by the MGE remains largely unknown.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and represents a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Pnoc may be a unique marker that distinguishes hippocampal interneurons from cortical interneurons.
source: Herein via scRNA-seq, we identified that Pnoc, a gene encoding prepronociceptin, may be a unique marker that distinguishes HINs from CINs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is based on scRNA-seq and FISH data showing Pnoc expression is restricted to HINs.

claim: Pnoc was previously described as an interneuron marker.
source: Pnoc was previously described as an IN marker (Russ et al., 2015; Spiegel et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature (Russ et al., 2015; Spiegel et al., 2014).

claim: In a scRNA-seq analysis from hippocampal tissue, Pnoc expression was found enriched in O-LM hippocampal interneurons.
source: In a more recent scRNA-seq analysis from hippocampal tissue, Pnoc expression was found enriched in O-LM HINs (Harris et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Harris et al., 2018).

claim: ISH analysis from P2 WTs demonstrated that Pnoc is widely and robustly expressed in hippocampal interneurons but not cortical interneurons.
source: Our ISH analysis from P2 WTs demonstrated that Pnoc is widely and robustly expressed in HINs but not CINs (Figure 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Pnoc expression is strongly upregulated in the hippocampus in the cDKO, consistent with evidence for increased hippocampal interneuron generation.
source: Furthermore, Pnoc expression is strongly upregulated in the hippocampus in the cDKO (Figure 5), consistent with evidence for increased HIN generation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 5.

claim: Maf and Mafb control the cortical interneuron/hippocampal interneuron ratio by putting a brake on hippocampal interneuron generation.
source: Altogether, our data suggests that Maf and Mafb control the CIN/HIN ratio by putting a brake on HIN generation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the data showing increased HIN generation in cDKOs.

claim: As a result of loss of Maf and Mafb, the cDKOs have a disproportionate number of hippocampal interneurons.
source: As a result, the cDKOs have a disproportionate number of HINs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the quantification data showing increased HIN density.

claim: In addition to controlling the SST/PV interneuron subtype fate decision, Maf and Mafb also control cortical interneuron/hippocampal interneuron regional fate determination.
source: Thus, in addition to controlling the SST/PV IN subtype fate decision, Maf and Mafb also control CIN/HIN regional fate determination.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the data showing altered CIN/HIN ratios in cDKOs.

claim: scRNA-seq data suggested that Cxcr4 expression was reduced in neonatal Maf cDKO MGE interneurons.
source: Our scRNA-seq data suggested that Cxcr4 expression was reduced in neonatal Maf cDKO MGE INs (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: FISH at P2 showed clear reduction of Cxcr4 expression in Maf cDKO, especially in the hippocampus.
source: Indeed, FISH at P2 showed clear reduction of Cxcr4 expression in Maf cDKO, especially in the hippocampus (CA1, CA3 and DG p=0.0159; Neocortex p<0.0001; t test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: Cxcr4 expression reduction starts as early as E15.5 in Maf cDKOs.
source: Cxcr4 expression reduction starts as early as E15.5 (p=0.012; t test) (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6 with statistical analysis.

claim: Reduced Cxcr4 expression provides evidence for a potential mechanism underlying premature interneuron entrance into the cortical plate.
source: These provide evidence for a potential mechanism underlying premature IN entrance into the cortical plate, that we reported previously (Pai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the observation of reduced Cxcr4 and previous findings of altered IN migration.

claim: Cxcr4 null mice did not show interneuron over-migration or over-production in the hippocampus.
source: Note that Cxcr4 null mice did not show IN over-migration or over-production in the hippocampus (Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2011; Stumm et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2011; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature (Sánchez-Alcañiz et al., 2011; Stumm et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2011; Li et al., 2008).

claim: Reduced Cxcr4 alone probably does not explain why Maf cDKOs have more hippocampal interneurons.
source: While lacking Cxcr4 in the cDKO would lead to disruption in the IN chemotactic migration, reduced Cxcr4 alone probably does not explain why Maf cDKOs have more HINs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from comparison to Cxcr4 null mice.

claim: Differential expression analysis suggested that Nrp1 is upregulated in the cDKO.
source: DE analysis suggested that Nrp1 is upregulated in the cDKO (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: FISH showed higher Nrp1 expression in the P2 cDKO hippocampus.
source: FISH showed higher Nrp1 expression in the P2 cDKO hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by FISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: Semaphorin binding to the Nrp1 receptor is implicated in MGE-derived interneuron migration away from the striatum.
source: Semaphorin binding to the Nrp1 receptor is implicated in MGE-derived IN migration away from the striatum (Marín et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Marín et al., 2001).

claim: Semaphorin/neuropilin signaling is implicated in the generation and migration of cortical interneurons.
source: Semaphorin/neuropilin signaling is also implicated the generation and migration of CINs (Andrews et al., 2017; Tamamaki et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature (Andrews et al., 2017; Tamamaki et al., 2003).

claim: An increase in Nrp1 expression alone is not sufficient to promote the increased hippocampal interneurons/cortical interneurons ratio.
source: These results suggest that an increase in Nrp1 expression alone is not sufficient to promote the increased HINs/CIN ratio.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from transplantation experiments where Nrp1 overexpression did not recapitulate the cDKO phenotype.

claim: Nrp1 is not only a receptor for semaphorins, but also for vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
source: Interestingly, Nrp1 is not only a receptor for semaphorins, but also for vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and represents established knowledge.

claim: VEGF is expressed in the developing cortex and may regulate interneuron migration.
source: There is evidence that VEGF is expressed in the developing cortex and may regulate IN migration (Barber et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Barber et al., 2018).

claim: VEGF functions include regulating neurogenesis, neuronal migration and axonal guidance.
source: Mackenzie and Ruhrberg et al. extensively reviewed the functions of VEGF in the nervous system (Mackenzie and Ruhrberg, 2012), which includes regulating neurogenesis (Jin et al., 2002), neuronal migration (Schwarz et al., 2004) and axonal guidance (Erskine et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature (Mackenzie and Ruhrberg, 2012; Jin et al., 2002; Schwarz et al., 2004; Erskine et al., 2011).

claim: In the developing mouse brainstem, VEGF guides somata migration of NRP1-expressing facial motor neurons.
source: In the developing mouse brainstem, VEGF guides somata migration of NRP1-expressing facial motor neurons (Schwarz et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Schwarz et al., 2004).

claim: In the visual system, VEGF serves as a chemoattractant to NRP1-expressing retinal ganglionic cells to promote contralateral axonal extension.
source: In the visual system, VEGF serves as a chemoattractant to NRP1-expressing retinal ganglionic cells to promote contralateral axonal extension (Erskine et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Erskine et al., 2011).

claim: VEGF-NRP1 binding works in conjunction with CXCR4-SDF1 to promote breast cancer cell invasion/metastasis.
source: Another study further suggested that VEGF-NRP1 binding works in conjunction with CXCR4-SDF1 to promote breast cancer cell invasion/metastasis (Bachelder et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Bachelder et al., 2002).

claim: Interactions between NRP1 and CXCR4 can guide interneuron migration, and in this context, increases in NPR1 signaling may guide interneurons to the hippocampus.
source: Thus, while the change of Cxcr4 and Nrp1 expression in the Maf cDKO alone does not provide a clear mechanism for why the mutant generates more HINs, we propose that interactions between NRP1 and CXCR4 can guide IN migration, and that in this context, increases in NPR1 signaling may guide INs to the hippocampus.
evidence: This is a speculative claim stated in the discussion based on comparison to other systems.

claim: Maf cDKOs exhibit frequent spike-and-wave-discharges similar to those described in mouse models of genetic absence type epilepsy.
source: EEG recordings from freely behaving mice showed that Maf cDKOs exhibit frequent spike-and-wave-discharges (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) similar to those that have been previously described in mouse models of genetic absence type epilepsy (Crunelli and Leresche, 2002; Paz et al., 2011; Sorokin et al., 2016; Sorokin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by EEG data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous literature.

claim: The cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying seizures in Maf cDKOs are multifaceted, and include the overall reductions in MGE-derived cortical and hippocampal interneurons in the adult Maf cDKO mutant.
source: The cellular and molecular mechanisms underlying this are undoubtedly multifaceted, and include the overall reductions in MGE-derived CINs and HINs in the adult Maf cDKO mutant (Pai et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is inferred from the observation of seizures and previous findings of IN loss.

claim: Several genes regulated by Maf and Mafb, including Mef2c, Snap25 and Npy, have mutations that could lead to seizures.
source: Furthermore, we identified several genes regulated by Maf and Mafb, including Mef2c, Snap25 and Npy, mutations of which could lead to seizures (Colmers and El Bahh, 2003; Harrington et al., 2016; Houenou et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citations to previous literature (Colmers and El Bahh, 2003; Harrington et al., 2016; Houenou et al., 2017).

claim: Human patients with Maf mutations exhibit seizures and intellectual disability.
source: Moreover, human patients with Maf mutations exhibit seizures and ID (Niceta et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and supported by citation to previous literature (Niceta et al., 2015).

claim: Maf and Mafb are key regulators of many disease genes that are responsible for balanced MGE SST and PV interneuron production, interneuron morphological maturation, and balanced MGE cortical and hippocampal interneuron production.
source: In summary, we identified genetic targets (e.g. Mef2c, Snap25, Cxcr4) that are downstream of Maf and Mafb. While Maf and Mafb themselves are not high confidence neuropsychiatric disease genes, they are key regulators of many disease genes that are responsible for balanced MGE SST and PV IN production (Mef2c), IN morphological maturation (Mef2c, Snap25), and balanced MGE CIN and HIN production (Cxcr4, Nrp1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and summarizes the findings of the study.

claim: ~22% of the Nkx2.1-Cre lineage cortical interneurons are Sp9 positive at P2.
source: Of note, here we report that ~22% of the Nkx2.1-Cre lineage CINs are Sp9 positive at P2.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is based on RNAscope quantification data.

claim: This is the first report to show Sp9 expression in cortical interneurons in the Nkx2.1-Cre lineage.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report to show Sp9 expression in CINs in the Nkx2.1-Cre lineage.
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and represents a novel finding.

claim: ~60% of the PV candidate hippocampal interneurons are Sp9 positive.
source: We agree that 22% may be an underestimate because of several reasons: (1) when we looked at the Sp9 expression in the hippocampus,~60% of the PV candidate INs are Sp9 positive
evidence: This claim is stated in the discussion and is based on RNAscope quantification data.
